concepts.name: Systematic judgment error
concepts.summary: Explain that a cognitive bias is a predictable, directional deviation from accurate or rational judgment, not just a random mistake.

concepts.name: Mental shortcuts (heuristics)
concepts.summary: Describe heuristics as fast, low-effort rules that usually work well but sometimes produce biased conclusions.

concepts.name: Confirmation bias
concepts.summary: Recognise and define the tendency to seek, notice and favour information that fits existing beliefs.

concepts.name: Anchoring effect
concepts.summary: Explain that an initial number or piece of information unduly pulls later estimates toward it.

concepts.name: Availability heuristic
concepts.summary: Explain that people judge how common or likely something is by how easily examples come to mind.

concepts.name: Bias as universal and unconscious
concepts.summary: State that everyone has biases, usually operating without awareness, so feeling objective is not proof of being objective.

misconceptions.text: Cognitive biases only affect unintelligent or uneducated people.
Heuristics are always wrong and should never be used.
If I know about a bias, I am automatically immune to it.

concepts.name: Spotting biases in everyday cases
concepts.summary: Identify which bias (confirmation, anchoring, availability) is at work in a short realistic scenario such as shopping, news or hiring.

concepts.name: Hindsight bias
concepts.summary: Explain that after learning an outcome people overestimate how predictable it was.

concepts.name: Overconfidence effect
concepts.summary: Describe how people's confidence in their judgments tends to exceed their actual accuracy.

concepts.name: Self-serving bias
concepts.summary: Apply the idea that people credit successes to themselves and blame failures on circumstances when analysing examples.

concepts.name: Framing effect
concepts.summary: Show how presenting the same information as gains or losses changes choices, using paired examples.

concepts.name: Simple debiasing habits
concepts.summary: Use basic strategies such as considering the opposite, pausing before deciding and seeking disconfirming evidence.

misconceptions.text: Hindsight makes past events look obvious because they really were obvious.
Confidence is a reliable signal that a judgment is correct.
Two descriptions with the same facts will lead to the same decision.

concepts.name: Dual-process account of judgment
concepts.summary: Analyse how fast intuitive and slow deliberate processing interact and where biases arise from the former going unchecked.

concepts.name: Representativeness and base rates
concepts.summary: Analyse how judging by similarity to a prototype leads people to ignore base rates, as in the Linda and taxi problems.

concepts.name: Conjunction fallacy
concepts.summary: Recognise and explain why a conjunction of events cannot be more probable than either event alone.

concepts.name: Loss aversion and sunk costs
concepts.summary: Analyse how losses weigh more than equal gains and how this drives sunk-cost and status-quo decisions.

concepts.name: Fundamental attribution error
concepts.summary: Analyse how observers overweight personality and underweight situation when explaining others' behaviour.

concepts.name: Bias blind spot
concepts.summary: Explain why people see bias in others more readily than in themselves and why introspection fails to detect it.

concepts.name: Structured debiasing techniques
concepts.summary: Select and apply methods such as pre-mortems, checklists, the outside view and independent estimates to counter particular biases.

misconceptions.text: Fast intuitive thinking is always biased and slow deliberate thinking is always correct.
A vivid description that fits a category makes that category more probable regardless of how rare it is.
Past investment is a valid reason to continue a project with poor prospects.

concepts.name: Heuristics and biases vs ecological rationality
concepts.summary: Evaluate the debate over whether heuristics are flaws or adaptive tools suited to particular environments.

concepts.name: Evaluating bias experiments
concepts.summary: Assess the design, effect sizes, replication status and ecological validity of classic bias studies such as anchoring and priming.

concepts.name: Bias in professional decisions
concepts.summary: Analyse how biases such as anchoring, premature closure and overconfidence shape decisions in fields like medicine, law and investing.

concepts.name: Group and organisational bias
concepts.summary: Analyse how group processes can amplify or dampen individual biases, as in groupthink and shared-information effects.

concepts.name: Motivated reasoning vs cognitive bias
concepts.summary: Distinguish biases arising from limited processing from those driven by goals, emotion or identity, and predict which remedies suit each.

concepts.name: Assessing debiasing effectiveness
concepts.summary: Evaluate evidence on which debiasing interventions work, how well they transfer, and when changing the environment beats training.

concepts.name: Choice architecture and nudges
concepts.summary: Evaluate how defaults and framing can exploit or counter biases, including ethical limits.

misconceptions.text: Every famous bias effect is large, universal and has replicated unchanged.
Training people about biases reliably improves their decisions in new situations.
Groups always cancel out individual biases through diversity of opinion.

concepts.name: Normative standards for rationality
concepts.summary: Judge which normative benchmarks (Bayesian, expected utility, bounded rationality) legitimately define an error in a given task.

concepts.name: Noise versus bias decomposition
concepts.summary: Evaluate judgment errors by separating systematic bias from random noise and choose remedies for each.

concepts.name: Bias-aware decision process design
concepts.summary: Design organisational decision procedures, such as independent assessments and structured criteria, that reduce bias and noise.

concepts.name: Theory integration of bias mechanisms
concepts.summary: Construct explanations that unify many biases through mechanisms like attribute substitution, limited memory and resource-rational trade-offs.

concepts.name: Designing bias studies
concepts.summary: Create rigorous studies that test a bias claim with proper controls, sufficient power and preregistration.

concepts.name: Algorithmic and AI bias interplay
concepts.summary: Evaluate how human cognitive biases enter data and models and how automation bias alters reliance on algorithmic output.

concepts.name: Individual and cultural variation
concepts.summary: Critique claims of universality by weighing evidence on individual differences, expertise and cross-cultural variation.

misconceptions.text: All deviations from textbook probability theory count as irrational errors regardless of the task.
Reducing bias is enough to make human judgments consistent and accurate.
Algorithms remove human bias because they are not subject to cognition.
